paragraphs.text: ReNU syndrome is a neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by intellectual disability, microcephaly, short stature, hypotonia, seizures, and motor delay (Greene et al., 2024). Chen et al. (2024) found moderate to severe global developmental delay and intellectual disability in all of the patients they phenotyped in detail. Most patients walked late and most were nonverbal. Nearly all had dysmorphic facial features, and many had abnormal brain MRI findings and visual, gastrointestinal, and skeletal involvement.

paragraphs.text: Greene et al. (2024) analyzed Human Phenotype Ontology (HPO) terms in 46 participants in the 100,000 Genomes Project who carried RNU4-2 variants and were coded with neurodevelopmental abnormality. Of these 46 cases, 91% had intellectual disability, 91% had neurodevelopmental delay, and 61% had motor delay. Several terms were significantly overrepresented compared with other cases coded with neurodevelopmental abnormality: microcephaly in 57% (vs 18%), drooling in 13% (vs 1%), proportionate short stature in 28% (vs 7%), generalized hypotonia in 39% (vs 13%), seizure in 52% (vs 27%), and abnormality of the upper lip vermilion in 13% (vs 2%). No terms were significantly underrepresented.

paragraphs.text: Chen et al. (2024) collected detailed phenotypic information on 49 individuals (21 females and 28 males; median age at last evaluation, 10 years; range, 2 to 38 years) with RNU4-2 variants. Of these, 42 had n.64_65insT, 3 had other single-base insertions, and 4 had single-nucleotide variants (SNVs). All had moderate to severe global developmental delay and intellectual disability. Of the individuals older than 5 years, 83% were ambulatory, but they walked late (average 3.4 years; range, 17 months to 7.5 years), and some had a wide-based or ataxic gait. Only 3 individuals had fluent speech; some had a few words, and most were nonverbal. Other features included short stature (37 of 49), microcephaly (37 of 48; mostly congenital), intrauterine growth restriction (8 of 45), hypotonia (39 of 45), seizures (37 of 48), behavioral issues (30 of 45), autism spectrum disorder (21 of 44), and sleep issues (15 of 32). Seizure onset varied, with a median of 3 years and a range from the first year of life to 10 years. Seizure types included infantile spasms, focal seizures, generalized tonic-clonic seizures, febrile seizures, and status epilepticus. Brain MRI was abnormal in 41 of 45 individuals. The most frequent findings were reduced white matter volume, hypoplasia of the corpus callosum, ventriculomegaly, delayed myelination, and other nonspecific white matter abnormalities. Visual issues (38 of 48) included optic nerve hypoplasia, cortical blindness, strabismus, and nystagmus. Gastrointestinal problems included constipation (29 of 44), gastroesophageal reflux (21 of 43), and feeding difficulties (32 of 42), with gastrostomy tubes in 13 of 41. Bone and/or skeletal abnormalities (27 of 42) included osteopenia, recurrent fractures, scoliosis, kyphosis, and hip dysplasia. Fewer individuals had hearing loss (10 of 46), endocrine problems (hypothyroidism, growth hormone deficiency, pituitary abnormalities), or limb, genitourinary, dental, cardiac, or cutaneous concerns. All but 3 individuals had dysmorphic facial features. These varied but included a myopathic face with deep-set eyes (some widely and some narrowly spaced), epicanthus, a wide nasal bridge, anteverted nares or underdeveloped alae nasi, and large cupped ears (some posteriorly rotated). Other facial features were full cheeks, a distinctive mouth with full lips and downturned corners, a high-arched palate, and a large or protruding tongue. No significant differences were noted between males and females.

paragraphs.text: Most RNU4-2 variants in ReNU syndrome occurred de novo (Greene et al., 2024; Schot et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2024). Chen et al. (2024) described the disorder as autosomal dominant. Greene et al. (2024) reported 1 proband who inherited the n.76C>T variant from an affected mother. They also found that the mother of a proband with n.65A>G was likely mosaic for the variant. Chen et al. (2024) reported 1 individual with a maternally inherited n.76C>T variant and 1 individual whose mother appeared mosaic for n.65A>G. They also reported 2 affected sibs who carried n.77_78insT. In all 54 individuals in whom the parental origin of the variant could be determined, the variant was on the maternal allele (Chen et al., 2024).

paragraphs.text: Greene et al. (2024) performed a rare-variant genetic association analysis of 41,132 noncoding genes using whole-genome sequencing data from the 100,000 Genomes Project. They compared 5,529 unrelated cases with intellectual disability with 46,401 unrelated controls. RNU4-2 had an extremely strong dominant association (posterior probability of association about 1), much stronger than that of any other noncoding gene. Three variants had a posterior probability of pathogenicity above 0.5. Five more variants within a few base pairs of these were also found only in affected participants, forming 2 contiguous regions (n.62-70 and n.73-79) in which no unaffected participant had a rare variant. These regions lay within a locus markedly depleted of variation in gnomAD. Of the 47 cases with variants in these regions, 37 were de novo, and inheritance was unknown in 10 because parental genotypes were missing. The most common variant, n.64_65insT, occurred de novo in 33 different families. Greene et al. (2024) replicated the findings in 3 further collections: the NIHR BioResource, the 100,000 Genomes Project Pilot, and the UK Genomic Medicine Service. In these collections they found 27 more probands with a rare variant in the 2 regions, of whom 26 were affected. Of the 26 affected probands, 19 had a de novo variant, 6 had a variant of unknown inheritance, and 1 inherited n.76C>T from an affected mother.

paragraphs.text: In the Genomics England 100,000 Genomes Project, Chen et al. (2024) identified a recurrent single-base insertion in RNU4-2 (n.64_65insT). It had arisen de novo in 38 probands sequenced with their unaffected parents and was found in 8 more probands, in all of whom the detectable inheritance was consistent with de novo occurrence. These 46 individuals made up 0.52% of 8,841 probands with undiagnosed NDD. The variant was absent from 3,408 diagnosed NDD probands, 21,817 non-NDD probands, 33,122 unaffected individuals, gnomAD v4.0, and the All of Us dataset, and it was seen in a single UK Biobank individual. Chen et al. (2024) then defined an 18-bp region of RNU4-2 (nucleotides 62-79) that was depleted of variation in population datasets. They identified heterozygous variants in this region in 115 individuals with NDD, 61 from Genomics England and 54 from other cohorts. Sequencing data for both parents were available for 86 of the 115 individuals, and these confirmed that the variants had arisen de novo. Most of the 115 individuals (89; 77.4%) had n.64_65insT, and a second insertion, n.77_78insT, was seen in 6 individuals, 2 of whom were affected sibs. Single-base insertions in the region were strongly enriched in undiagnosed NDD probands compared with UK Biobank participants (OR = 1,531). SNVs across the region were modestly enriched (OR = 9.51), and those found in patients clustered at the 2 ends of the critical region. SNVs in the central portion, particularly at nucleotides 71 to 74, were also found in non-NDD individuals and population controls. Chen et al. (2024) also tested other brain-expressed snRNA genes, and none was significantly enriched for de novo or recessive variants in undiagnosed NDD probands.

paragraphs.text: Chen et al. (2024) noted that the critical region maps to the T-loop (quasi-pseudoknot) and stem III of the U4/U6 duplex. The 5-prime splice sites with increased use showed more T at position +3 and more C at positions +4 and +5. These positions pair directly with U6 ACAGAGA, which the authors considered functional evidence that the variants disrupt accurate splice-site recognition. Chen et al. (2024) also found that RNU4-2 is consistently expressed at higher levels than RNU4-1 in the developing human prefrontal cortex, with greater chromatin accessibility in prenatal cortex. This supported RNU4-2 as the main U4 transcript in the brain.
